street.note: The maintainer's observation, July 2026; prices for this card are all over the place. The reference post (2025) cites one Bilibili buyer at 2,200 yuan (about $305 then), and its author bought four on eBay at an unstated "bargain" price.

power.note: Load is the post author's figure under a gpu-fryer matmul burn (not LLM inference) with the card held at 1,140 MHz, "the lowest it accepts"; the card has no power limit ("the cards don't support power limiting AT ALL"), so downclocking is the only cap, and the author says an unclocked card "can draw 600W if it wants to" (not measured on the page). Idle is the post's nvidia-smi screenshot: 40-45 W across four cards in P0 with Xorg attached.

units.note: Bandwidth: the source table says "1433Gbps", read here as GB/s. 1,433 Gbit/s would be 179 GB/s, less than one HBM2 stack, and 32 GB of HBM2 as four 8 GB stacks (4,096 bits) at 2.8 Gbit/s per pin gives 1,433.6 GB/s; the post itself reads it as "1.4TBps". INT8: NVIDIA does not say whether 900 TOPS is dense or sparse, and the post's author flags the same doubt ("sparsity??"). It is filed as sparse because a dense 900 is out of reach for GA100: dense INT8 is 4,096 ops per clock per SM, so 900 TOPS needs about 2.0 GHz on 108 SMs or 1.7 GHz on all 128, against 1.41 GHz on every datacenter A100. That is an inference, not a published fact. No dense figure is recorded, so this card has no INT8 prefill ceiling. Measured: the post's gpu-fryer run reads 207 TFLOPS per card at 1,140 MHz (precision not shown; the author reports "around 250TF" at stock clocks, not shown). It must be a 16-bit rate, since GA100 TF32 cannot reach it, and it shows the die is not GA102. The same holds for HBM2, which among Ampere dies only GA100 has. A measurement is a floor, not a rating, so it is not stored as a ceiling. Board: SXM2-format with 36 mm heatsink holes, not the standard 32 mm. NVLink does not work: the GSP reports no NVLink support, and the author understands the board lacks the traces ("the chip supports NVLINK but the pcb misses the NVLINK traces"). Rated PCIe 4.0 x16; it ran at PCIe 3.0 on the post's AOM-SXMV carrier. Do not substitute datacenter A100 SXM4 figures: the memory, interconnect and form factor all differ. MLPerf Inference v2.0 (Edge, Closed, ID 2.0-112) lists an "NVIDIA Drive-A100-PCIe"; that is a PCIe variant running non-LLM benchmarks, so it is not used here.

The Tesla table gives one row for the 16 GB and 32 GB SXM2 parts; clocks, bandwidth and throughput are identical across both, so only the capacity differs. The release date is the 32 GB part's (announced March 2018), not the 16 GB module's May 2017; the shared row dates the product line. FP16 is the tensor-core rate with FP32 accumulate — Volta has no structured-sparsity path. No INT8 figure recorded: Volta's Tensor Cores are hard-wired FP16-input/FP32-accumulate only -- NVIDIA's own current Tensor Core page attributes full FP32/FP16/INT8/INT4 inference precision support to Turing onward, not Volta. No official DP4A/integer-ALU INT8 figure was ever published for V100 either (the Volta architecture whitepaper gives an INT8 figure for sibling Pascal parts P40/P4 but conspicuously omits one for V100). Unsourced ~62-63 TOPS figures circulating on aggregator sites appear to be an unofficial 4x-of-FP32 estimate, not a published spec -- not used. Also lacks BF16 (arrived with Ampere, later still than Turing) -- the same FP16-input/FP32-accumulate-only tensor path that rules out INT8 rules out BF16 too. Software support is ending: CUDA 13 cannot target Volta, R580 is its last driver branch (supported to June 2028), and PyTorch 2.14 is the last release with Volta wheels; see the volta generation.

peerLink.fabric: NVLink 2 on an SXM2 baseboard (DGX-1 / HGX-1, or IBM Power AC922 with POWER9 CPUs)
peerLink.topology: DGX-1 / HGX-1, 8 GPUs: hybrid cube-mesh, not all-to-all, six 50 GB/s links per GPU (300 GB/s bidirectional), each GPU wired to 4 of the other 7; collectives relay through neighbours. IBM AC922, 4 or 6 GPUs: two or three per POWER9, wired to each other and to their CPU by NVLink (3 bricks per link with two per CPU, 2 with three); GPUs on different sockets reach each other through both CPUs and the 64 GBps X Bus, still without PCIe
peerLink.source: https://images.nvidia.com/content/pdf/dgx1-v100-system-architecture-whitepaper.pdf -- "Each Tesla V100 has 6 NVLink connections, each capable of 50 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, for an aggregate of up to 300 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth. ... Figure 4 DGX-1 uses an 8-GPU hybrid cube-mesh interconnection network topology. ... Furthermore, this 8-GPU cube-mesh topology is easily subdivided into fully connected halves, or into NVLink-connected GPU pairs."
peerLink.note: A single SXM2 module on a PCIe adapter, the usual hobbyist setup, has no NVLink at all. The AC922 cross-socket path is a 64 GBps bidirectional SMP bus, about what PCIe 4.0 x16 gives, so its 4- and 6-GPU groups are joined without PCIe but not at NVLink speed. IBM Redpaper REDP-5472 (Power AC922 Introduction and Technical Overview), p.15: "six connected GPUs, where the six NVLINK Bricks are divided into three groups of two Bricks, enabling 100 GBps buses between GPUs"; p.14: "four GPUs, where the six NVLINK Bricks are divided into groups of three, which enables 150 GBps buses between GPUs"; p.12: "Each POWER9 CPU and each GPU have six NVLINK channels, called Bricks, with each one delivering up to 50 GBps bidirectional bandwidth"; Figures 2-5 and 2-6 show the POWER9s joined by an "X Bus 64 GBps".

The only public PVC/llama.cpp number found anywhere is one changelog row (2025.2): Max 1550 going 39->73 tok/s on llama-2-7b Q4_0 -- 18-months-stale, on the flagship rather than this SKU, and roughly a tenth of an Arc A770's memory-bandwidth efficiency (the A770 posts 55-67 tok/s on a sixth of the bandwidth). The software stack has matured a lot since PVC's 2022 launch -- SYCL flash-attention (native and oneDNN-fused) landed 2026.03, and split-mode tensor (true tensor parallelism, not just layer-splitting) is explicitly 'optimized for 2 GPUs,' a good match for a 2-card 96GB build -- but nobody has published it running at depth. GGML_SYCL_FA_ONEDNN_MAX_KV exists specifically because 'GPU driver watchdog resets (DEVICE_LOST) occur during long-context inference,' with a documented workaround capping context near 24,576 tokens -- below this page's own long-context framing. Intel's own ARK listing gives this SKU's expected discontinuance as Jan 2026 (already past as of Aug 2026), which is presumably why pulled cards are turning up on eBay around $2,000 -- cheap for 48GB of HBM2e with real XMX matrix engines, expensive to be the first person to actually measure it at 128K context. Memory arithmetic: Intel's datasheet (817799) says three enabled 16 GB HBM2e stacks at 3.2 GT/s and, in its block diagram, '1.6 TB/s peak BW'; the package physically carries four stacks with one permanently disabled, so 1.6 TB/s is the four-stack figure and three stacks at the standard 1,024 bits give the 1,228.8 GB/s recorded here. PCIe 5.0 x16 to the host.

compute.note: Nothing here is Intel's rating for this card: Intel's product brief (revised 2025-11) lists Xe-cores, memory, cache, TDP and Xe Link but no throughput, and ARK lists none. FP64 and FP32 are Wikipedia's template figures and reproduce exactly from the shader count on the vector engines: 7,168 ALUs x 2 FLOP/clock x 1.55 GHz = 22.22 (Ponte Vecchio runs FP64 at the FP32 rate; see the Max 1550 for the measurement that confirms it). The matrix figures are derived: Intel's oneAPI GPU Optimization Guide gives 4,096 FP16/BF16 and 8,192 INT8 XMX ops per clock per Xe-core, times 56 Xe-cores at 1.55 GHz. TF32 is half the FP16 rate, as Intel's own 419 TFLOPS for the Max 1550 implies (128 Xe-cores x 2,048 x 1.6 GHz = 419.4), and as ALCF's measured GEMMs show. Wikipedia's template gives 352 BF16, about 1% below this arithmetic, for no stated reason. flopper.io's 420 / 839 / 210 for this card would need a 1.83 GHz clock and look like half the Max 1550's; they are not used. Which precisions the XMX engines take: Intel's SYCL matrix extension lists signed and unsigned INT8, FP16, BF16 and TF32 on intel_gpu_pvc, with no INT4, FP8 or FP4 entry, and oneDNN's data-type table marks f8, f4_e2m1 and s4/u4/u2 as conversion-only on Xe-HPC, so INT4 and FP8 are storage formats here, not compute rates.

units.note: Reference only -- and unlike the Max 1100 beside it, not a card you can buy or fit. This is a 600W OAM module, not a PCIe add-in card: it needs an OAM baseboard and the cooling to match, the same way an H100 SXM does, so 128GB in one package is academic for a workstation build no matter what it costs. No price is recorded because none was found -- Max Series went through OEM/integrator channels rather than retail, and unlike the 1100 (which turns up pulled on eBay around $2,000 post-EOL) the flagship has no observed secondary market at all. Included because 128GB of HBM2e at 3.28 TB/s in a single package is a genuinely interesting anchor for this page's 96-128GB class: it is the capacity target hit in one module, at roughly 2.7x an RTX PRO 6000's bandwidth. The public measured PVC numbers are ALCF's single-node GEMM runs on Aurora (Glenn Lockwood's page quotes an earlier version of them). They are per stack, half this card, so they sit at roughly 63-68% of the per-stack peak, not the 30-35% of whole-card peak this note used to say; the compute note has them. They are HPC GEMM kernels rather than LLM inference, and they stay out of compute.values because that column is rated throughput, not achieved. Intel's ARK listing gives expected discontinuance as Jan 2026.

compute.note: FP64 and FP32 run on the vector engines at the same rate: 16,384 ALUs x 2 FLOP/clock x 1.6 GHz = 52.43, against Intel's SC22 headline of 52. TF32 419 is Intel's own launch figure. FP16, BF16 and INT8 are derived, not rated: Intel's oneAPI GPU Optimization Guide gives 4,096 FP16/BF16 and 8,192 INT8 XMX ops per clock per Xe-core, times 128 Xe-cores at 1.6 GHz; the same arithmetic at 2,048 TF32 ops per clock reproduces Intel's 419. Intel's product brief lists no throughput figures. Wikipedia's template gives 832 BF16, 0.8% below this, and 54.423 FP32, which is a typo (its base-clock 29.491 is exact: 16,384 x 2 x 0.9 GHz). Measured on Aurora by ALCF (one stack, i.e. half this card, at the 1.5 GHz default, 2026-08-25): HGEMM 248, BF16 GEMM 255, TF32 GEMM 125 and INT8 GEMM 537 TFLOP/s, the 1 : 1 : 1/2 : 2 ratio of Intel's per-clock figures, at 63-68% of the per-stack peak at that clock (393 FP16, 197 TF32, 786 INT8). With all 12 stacks of a node busy, per-card throughput falls further: HGEMM 2,369 per six-card node is about 395 per card, half the derived peak at 1.5 GHz. ALCF's FP64 FMA chain reaches 16 TFLOP/s per stack, above the 12.3 a half-rate FP64 unit could reach at 1.5 GHz; that confirms the 1:1 rate, although the same Intel guide says 128 FP64 ops per clock per Xe-core, which is half rate.

compute.note: Derived, not rated: NVIDIA never published a rating for this card. Each figure is A100's dense per-SM tensor rate (whitepaper) x 70 SMs x 1,470 MHz, the sustained clock of an 8 GB card on the 300 W VBIOS, the same configuration as the bandwidth. The unlocked cards' own mma throughput lands just under these (satspace: BF16 201.55, INT8 409.77, TF32 99.82). Through torch, cuBLAS or OpenCL, INT8 measured only 43-48 TOPS in July 2026, against 335-410 TOPS in mma microbenchmarks; that gap is unresolved. llama.cpp issues mma directly, so the higher figure is the bound. No FP8, FP6 or FP4 (sm_80). Sparse rates were never measured on this card, so none are recorded. With 170tune’s qualified +250 MHz offset the SM clock reaches about 1,490-1,590 MHz near 250-280 W, up to 8% above the clock these figures assume; real prefill sits far below either.

units.note: A GA100 mining card that becomes a 64 GB inference card through a community unlock (cmpunlocker). The unlock patches the NVIDIA open kernel modules to address the HBM2e already on the card, 4 stacks of 16 GB on a 4096-bit bus, and to lift the compute throttle that left stock cards at 1/32 issue rate. Caveats: only the 8 GB card (PCI 10de:20c2) unlocks to 64 GB; the 10 GB card (10de:2082) reaches 40 GB, and nvidia-smi does not tell them apart. CUDA allocates about 63.4 GiB. Bandwidth depends on the card's VBIOS: 1,769 GB/s is the 300 W image (HBM at 1,728 MHz); the stock 250 W image runs 1,458 MHz for 1,493 GB/s. Both ship under the same ID, and the ceiling takes the faster. The patched driver pins exact versions (610.43.02/.03, 610.57.04, 615.71.09, 615.78.08 as of 2026-10-07), needs Secure Boot off and a cold power cycle, and is Linux-only. ECC is fused off; cmpunlocker reports it enabled since 2026-10-04, but nobody has shown it correcting errors, and one card needed a single-bit HBM page blacklisted by hand. The host link is PCIe Gen1 x4 stock. Gen2 comes from software, x16 from hand-soldering 24 missing capacitors, and Gen3 is unsolved. There is no NVLink. Memory and SM overclocks can corrupt data silently. Passively cooled, on a single EPS 8-pin.

candidates.label: 4× V100 SXM2 32GB on the 1CatAI board

interconnect.note: NVIDIA rates the SXM2 V100 at 300 GB/s of NVLink 2.0 per GPU (six links). Whether the 1CatAI carrier wires all six per GPU, its topology, and whether peer-to-peer is enabled are not verified; the NVLink itself is taken from this page's own platform label (V100 NVLink x4). The board costs $800: the maintainer's observation of multiple eBay listings at that price, with a cheaper source possible.

host.note: A mostly self-contained, eGPU-like device (the maintainer's description): unlike the PCIe-card rigs it does not lean on the host for per-card slots, spacing or power in the same way. Its uplink and power supply are not yet sourced.

candidates.note: The engine in play is 1Cat-vLLM, a one-team vLLM fork for SM70. The only report so far is one unreproduced GitHub issue (1CatAI/1Cat-vLLM#746), which describes a different variant: four PCIe cards, no NVLink, 200 W caps. The stack is a dead end upstream: CUDA 13, PyTorch after 2.14 and upstream vLLM all exclude Volta, so this rig stays on CUDA 12.x, the R580 driver branch (supported to June 2028) and SM70 forks.

candidates.label: 4× Instinct MI100 32GB with an Infinity Fabric bridge

interconnect.note: AMD: three Infinity Fabric links per GPU, up to 276 GB/s peer-to-peer per GPU and 552 GB/s for a four-GPU hive, all theoretical peaks; PCIe Gen4 x16 (64 GB/s) to the host. Bridges have been seen at $650 to $1,200; the low figure sets the main total.

host.note: PCIe cards, so the host supplies everything: a power supply for 4 x 300 W of passively cooled, full-height dual-slot cards and, ideally, four x16 slots of PCIe 4.0 or better with spacing for the Infinity Fabric bridge. Host requirements are the maintainer's; card power, slot size and cooling are AMD's brochure. The host is not priced.

candidates.note: Passively cooled, full-height dual-slot, 300 W each (AMD brochure): the rig needs server airflow. Which engines run the model's recurrent layers on gfx908 is unknown here; llama.cpp HIP and vLLM-ROCm are the obvious ones and specialist engines may exist. Continued ROCm support for gfx908 is a risk raised in the program's planning notes, not verified here.

candidates.label: 2× Data Center GPU Max 1100 48GB with an Xe Link bridge

interconnect.note: Intel datasheet 817799: each card has six 53 Gbps SerDes ports. The X2 bridge (99ARXG) joins two cards with six Xe Link connections between them; the X4 bridge (99ARXX) gives each pair of four cards two. The datasheet states no GB/s: whether a connection is one lane or several changes the aggregate about eightfold, so none is recorded. Host link is PCIe 5.0 x16 at 32 GT/s (128 GB/s counted AMD's way; about 63 GB/s per direction after encoding). A separate Xe Link Bridge Card Datasheet (788941) should state the bandwidth and could not be found. The two-card bridge usually ships with a pair of cards and costs about $70 when bought separately. The maintainer has never seen a four-card (X4) bridge for sale, so a four-card rig is not purchasable as far as is known.

host.note: PCIe cards, so the host supplies everything: two x16 slots, ideally PCIe 5.0, spaced for the two-card Xe Link bridge, and a supply with a CEM 5.1 12V-2x6 auxiliary connector per card at up to 300 W each (Intel datasheet 817799). Slot and spacing needs are the maintainer's. The host is not priced.

candidates.note: Two cards split two KV heads cleanly under tensor parallel. The catalog unit records that no public Max 1100 llama.cpp datapoints existed as of Aug 2026; engines in play include llama.cpp SYCL and vLLM-XPU.

candidates.label: 4× PG199 / DRIVE A100 on a Supermicro AOM-SXMV

interconnect.bridge: Supermicro AOM-SXMV 4× SXM2 carrier (PCIe switches; NVLink unused)
interconnect.note: Cost covers the carrier and the parts it cannot run without, at the post's 2025 prices before VAT, shipping and buying-agent fees. The carrier is about $690 (no AOM-SXMV below 5,000 yuan on Xianyu when the author came to buy, down from about 2,000 yuan earlier) to $900 (a Supermicro refurbished-parts quote, two-unit minimum). On top of that: a case with fans and a 1,400 W power supply (about $300), two JPCIE-to-PCIe cables (about $20 each) and four heatsinks (about $20 each). The high end adds four $50 brackets for the PG199's 36 mm heatsink-hole spacing, which the author avoided by filing the heatsinks by hand. NVLink does not work on these cards, so peers talk over PCIe. The post's cards ran at PCIe 3.0 x16 at best, two GPUs sharing each of the carrier's switches, and slower behind a bifurcated host slot. The host link is therefore PCIe 3.0 x16, not the card's rated 4.0.

host.note: Two host x16 slots feed the carrier, one per switch. The post's Ryzen 9 7950X has 24 CPU lanes, which forced bifurcation and slowed the second pair ("I should have at least 32"). The case supplies the GPUs' power independently of the host. The host is not priced.

candidates.note: One person's documented build, used for RL work, not LLM serving, so there are no inference figures. The cards have no power limit: the author holds them at 1,140 MHz, the lowest clock they accept, for about 250 W each, and says an unclocked card "can draw 600W if it wants to". The four cards on the 1,400 W supply only fit with the downclock. The author also suspects dried thermal paste under the heat spreader, and Xianyu sellers list delidded cards. Card supply and prices vary widely.
